prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a close, uneven rock wall spanning the left and centre in frames 1–3, with the rope and metal anchor in frame 3 much nearer than the surrounding rock, approximately 0.3–0.8 m from the camera; the bright opening above/right is unreliable as metric depth because sky and high contrast can saturate monocular estimates. In frame 4, one person stands below and to the right/front of the camera wearer, roughly 2–4 m away, while the rock face is closer on the right and the passage extends farther behind them. In frame 5, the camera wearer’s raised hand is within arm’s reach, about 0.2–0.5 m away, and partly occludes a person approximately 1–2 m ahead who faces generally toward the camera; another person is only partly visible at the far-right edge and appears several metres farther away. Across the frames the viewpoint turns from the nearby wall and hanging ropes toward the open passage and people, while near objects become brighter and more clearly separated than they are in RGB; exact metre estimates, thin ropes, dark recesses, and object boundaries remain unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates no dependable instances in frames 1–2, then separates two prominent foreground regions in frame 3, but labels the climbing hardware/rope and rock opening as “bird” and “broccoli,” so those classes are clearly unreliable despite providing useful silhouettes and occlusion boundaries. In frame 4 it isolates one person in the lower-right/central area, roughly 2–4 m in front of the wearer, with no other person mask nearby. In frame 5 it separates a nearer person around 1–2 m ahead from another person clipped by the far-right image boundary and likely several metres away; the two people are separated laterally by several metres in the scene, and the nearer person appears oriented toward the camera wearer. The masks make the people and their partial out-of-frame extent easier to distinguish than in RGB, but they omit the wearer’s close raised hand, ropes, most rock surfaces, and body orientation details, and the changing masks mainly reflect the camera turning right rather than reliable object tracking.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only a magenta hand skeleton in frame 5, positioned high on the right side of that frame and corresponding to the camera wearer’s raised hand roughly 0.2–0.5 m away and above the nearer person. Its articulated finger layout makes the hand’s orientation and within-reach position clearer than RGB, while also showing that it partly blocks the view beyond it. No body skeletons are recovered for the person 2–4 m ahead in frame 4 or for either person in frame 5, so their exact facing direction, gaze, limb positions, mutual reach, and separation cannot be established from this map; RGB only suggests that the nearer frame-5 person faces generally toward the wearer. The absence of poses in frames 1–4 and failure to represent the visible people make this map unreliable for temporal approach, retreat, or turning, beyond showing that the wearer’s hand enters the view in the final frame.
